title: Processes and system calls
objectives: Explain a process, a system call and a context switch, and what each costs.

screens.title: Where the program waits
screens.prose: A program reads one packet and prints it. `strace -T` lists each system call and, in angle brackets, the seconds it took. This trace is abbreviated and invented in our own words, not a real log.
screens.question: Tap the call where the program waits.

hints.text: Which call took far longer than the others?
`<0.012340>` is 12.34 ms, over a thousand times the rest.
Line 3, the `recvfrom`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the times in angle brackets.

byKey.l1: `socket` took 12 µs. It only makes a descriptor.
byKey.l2: `bind` took 8 µs, about the same as `socket`.
byKey.l4: `write` took 10 µs, the same order as `socket` and `bind`.

explain.text: `recvfrom` took 12.34 ms because the thread slept until a packet arrived. The other calls took about 10 µs each. A call that blocks hands the core to another thread until it can finish.

screens.title: Read a megabyte
screens.prose: A **system call** asks the kernel to act for your program. Round figure: one call costs about 0.2 µs on a modern core. Slide the read size and watch the calls.

derive.caption: {{money(1048576 / chunk, '', 0)}} calls of {{money(chunk, '', 0)}} bytes: {{money(1048576 / chunk * 0.2, '', 1)}} µs of call overhead.

screens.question: How many calls does 64 KiB per read need for the whole 1 MiB?

hints.text: Divide the 1 MiB by the bytes per read.
1 MiB is 1,048,576 bytes and 64 KiB is 65,536.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Calls are the file size over the bytes per read.

byKey.small: 16,384 is the count for 64-byte reads. Slide to 64 KiB.
byKey.mid: 256 is the count for 4 KiB reads. Slide to 64 KiB.

explain.text: A 64 KiB read is 1,024 times bigger than a 64-byte read, so it needs 1,024 times fewer calls. Sixteen calls cost 3.2 µs; sixteen thousand would cost 3,276.8 µs.

screens.title: Count the calls
screens.prose: Now without the slider. The file is 1 MiB, 1,048,576 bytes, and every call costs 0.2 µs. Work from the number of calls.
screens.question: Fill in the calls and the overhead.

rows: Times fewer calls: 64 KiB reads against 64-byte reads

hints.text: Calls are the file size over the read size.
16,384 and 3,276.8 µs; 256 and 51.2 µs; 64 KiB needs 16 calls, so 1,024 times fewer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

explain.text: Calls fall in proportion to the read size: 16,384, then 256, then 16. The overhead is 3,276.8 µs with 64-byte reads and 51.2 µs with 4 KiB reads. Batch your reads.

screens.title: A wake for every message
screens.prose: A **context switch** changes which thread runs on a core. Round figure: 2 µs each. A thread that sleeps on a socket and is woken per message pays two: one to sleep, one to wake.

lines: thread: recv() with nothing to read
kernel: sleep this thread, run another
kernel: wake this thread, run it again
params.title: One blocking receive

screens.question: Fill in the cost of waking once per message.

rows: Share of a core at 100,000 messages a second

hints.text: Count one switch to sleep and one to wake.
$2 \times 2\ \mu s = 4\ \mu s$ a message.
$100{,}000 \times 4\ \mu s = 0.4$ s of every second: 40%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: One switch to sleep and one to wake.

explain.text: Two switches of 2 µs cost 4 µs a message. At 100,000 messages a second that is 0.4 s of every second, 40% of a core, before any real work.

screens.title: Process or thread
screens.prose:
A **process** is a program with its own address space and its own file-descriptor table. Threads of one process share both. `fork` makes a child process that starts as a copy.

```cpp
int x = 5;
if (fork() == 0) x = 9;   // the child
```
screens.question: After `fork`, the child sets `x = 9`. What does the parent's `x` show, and why?

options.text: Still 5: the child wrote to its own copy of the page
9: parent and child share the variable
options.why: You treated the child as a thread. A process has its own address space, so the write cannot reach the parent.

options.text: 5, because `fork` copies all memory before it returns
options.why: Copying everything up front would be slow. The frames are shared until one side writes.

options.text: Either: the two processes race on `x`
options.why: A race needs shared memory. After the write the two copies are separate.

hints.text: Do two processes share an address space?
The table shows one address space for threads and one each for processes.
The child gets its own copy of that page when it writes.

feedback.correct: Still 5: the write went to the child's own copy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the address space row of the table.

byKey.shared: That is how two threads behave. Two processes have separate address spaces.
byKey.early: The frames are shared at first, and copied only on a write.
byKey.race: There is no shared variable to race on once the child has written.

explain.text: The child's write gives it its own copy of that one page, so the parent still sees 5. Until a write, parent and child share the same frames: this is **copy-on-write**. Two threads would have shared `x` and both seen 9.

screens.title: Is a call a switch
screens.prose: A colleague says every system call is a context switch, so calls cost as much as switches.

lines: -> user mode, thread A carries on
params.title: One system call

screens.question: Is a system call a context switch?

options.text: No: the same thread carries on, in kernel mode
Yes: the kernel runs, so the thread is switched out
options.why: The kernel runs on your thread's behalf. No other thread was scheduled.

options.text: Yes, and it costs about 2 µs
options.why: A switch to another thread costs 2 µs. A call costs about 0.2 µs, ten times less.

options.text: No, and it costs nothing at all
options.why: It costs about 0.2 µs each: 16,384 of them cost about 3.3 ms.

hints.text: Which thread is running before and after the call?
The same thread A writes before and after.
Only its privilege level changes.

feedback.correct: No: one thread, two privilege levels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does any other thread run during the call?

byKey.yes: Nothing else was scheduled. The same thread went into the kernel and came back.
byKey.yes2: The 2 µs is a thread switch. A call is ten times cheaper.
byKey.free: Each call costs about 0.2 µs, and thousands of them add up.

explain.text: A system call changes the privilege level of the same thread, so it costs about 0.2 µs. A context switch changes which thread runs and costs about 2 µs. A call that blocks, like `recvfrom` earlier, causes a switch too.

screens.title: A call with no kernel entry
screens.prose: Some calls never enter the kernel. Linux keeps the time in a shared page, so `clock_gettime` reads it in user space in about 20 ns. Round figure.
screens.question: How many milliseconds do 500,000 such reads take?

widget.accept: 10 ms: 500,000 × 20 ns. As real system calls they would take 100 ms.

hints.text: Multiply the count by 20 ns.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count 20 ns for each read, not 200 ns.

byKey.kernel: That is 500,000 reads at 200 ns, as if each entered the kernel. This read does not.
byKey.slip: You slipped a power of ten. 10,000,000 ns is 10 ms.

explain.text: The shortcut costs 20 ns a read, so 500,000 reads take 10 ms. A real system call would cost about 200 ns here and 100 ms in all. Not every library call is a system call.

screens.title: The cost of a call
screens.prose:
Reading a file in pieces costs

$$\text{overhead} = \frac{\text{bytes}}{\text{bytes per call}} \times 0.2\ \mu s.$$

Read *Beej's Guide to Network Programming* (a free guide) and the Linux manual pages for `read`, `recv` and `epoll`.
screens.question: Doubling the bytes per call does what to the overhead?

options.why: The bytes copied stay the same, but the number of calls does not.
You multiplied by the read size. It sits under the bar, so doubling it halves the cost.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The read size is the divisor.

byKey.same: The count of calls changes with the read size, and so does the overhead.
byKey.double: The read size divides the bytes. A bigger read means fewer calls.

explain.text: Overhead is calls times 0.2 µs, and calls are the bytes over the read size. A bigger read means fewer calls. The copying does not shrink, only the entries into the kernel.

screens.title: Drill: calls and switches
screens.prose: Drill: about two minutes each. Say the reasoning aloud first. Round figures: a call 0.2 µs, a thread switch 2 µs, and a wake per message costs two switches.
screens.question: Fill in each answer.

rows: One wake per message at 250,000 a second: cores spent on switching

hints.text: Calls are the size over the read size.
4 MiB is 4,194,304 bytes; 8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes.
1,024 and 204.8 µs; 128 and 25.6 µs; $250{,}000 \times 4\ \mu s = 1$ s a second.

feedback.correct: 1,024, 204.8 µs, 128, 25.6 µs and one whole core.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r4c1: Two switches of 2 µs is 4 µs a message: 250,000 × 4 µs is 1 s.

explain.text: Calls are bytes over read size, and overhead is calls times 0.2 µs. At 250,000 messages a second the wake-ups alone fill a whole core. Batching and avoiding wake-ups are the two fixes.

screens.title: Follow-up: recv per message
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: your handler calls `recv` for every 24-byte message, at 200,000 messages a second. A datagram carries up to 1,472 bytes, which is 61 frames of 24 bytes with 8 bytes spare.
screens.question: What does that cost, and what does packing save?

rows: Time spent in calls each second (ms)
Calls a second if each datagram holds 61 frames

hints.text: Multiply the rate by 0.2 µs.
$200{,}000 \times 0.2\ \mu s = 40$ ms in every second.
40 ms of 1,000 ms is 4%. Then $200{,}000 / 61$, rounded up, is 3,279 calls.

feedback.correct: 40 ms, 4% of a core, 3,279 calls a second.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

explain.text: 200,000 calls of 0.2 µs take 40 ms of every second, 4% of a core. Packing 61 frames to a datagram cuts that to 3,279 calls, about 0.07% of a core. On a desk, batching reads comes before anything cleverer.

ideas: A system call asks the kernel to act and returns to the same thread: about 0.2 µs. A context switch changes the thread: about 2 µs.
Batch your reads: a 64 KiB read needs 1,024 times fewer calls than a 64-byte read.
Threads share an address space and a descriptor table; processes do not. `fork` copies a page only when someone writes.

formula.name: Call overhead
formula.note: Round figure for a modern core.

summary.trap: Counting every system call as a context switch.

quiz.prose: A thread reads a 2 MiB file in 32 KiB reads. One system call costs 0.2 µs.
quiz.question: How many microseconds of call overhead does the whole read cost?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls first, then multiply by 0.2 µs.

byKey.calls: 64 is the number of calls. Multiply by 0.2 µs.

explain.text: 2 MiB is 2,097,152 bytes, and 32 KiB is 32,768, so 64 calls. At 0.2 µs each that is 12.8 µs.

quiz.prose: A trading loop timestamps every message.
quiz.question: Which of these does not enter the kernel?

options.text: Reading the clock through the shared page

options.why: A write is a system call: the kernel owns the socket.
Opening a file is a system call: the kernel owns the file system.
A receive is a system call, and may also block.

feedback.correct: Only the clock shortcut stays in user space.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which call reads a page the kernel keeps updated?

explain.text: The kernel keeps the time in a shared page, so the read needs no kernel entry. Writes, opens and receives all do.

quiz.prose: One thread of a process opens a file and receives descriptor 4.
quiz.question: Can another thread of the same process read descriptor 4?

options.text: Yes: the descriptor table belongs to the process
No: each thread has its own descriptor table
options.why: Threads share the table. Only a separate process has its own.

options.text: Only after the first thread calls `fork`
options.why: `fork` makes a new process with its own table. It is not needed to share between threads.

feedback.correct: Yes: threads share the process's table.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a process own that its threads share?

explain.text: The descriptor table belongs to the process, so every thread of it sees descriptor 4. A forked child gets a copy of the table instead.

quiz.prose: A thread is woken for every message, at 50,000 messages a second. A switch costs 2 µs and each message needs two.
quiz.question: What share of a core goes on switching?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two switches of 2 µs make 4 µs a message.

byKey.half: You counted one switch a message. Waking and sleeping make two.

explain.text: Two switches of 2 µs are 4 µs a message. At 50,000 a second that is 0.2 s of every second, 20% of a core.
